title: Systems with Repeated Eigenvalues
short: Find a generalized eigenvector when one is missing.

blocks.html: Sometimes a $2\times 2$ matrix has one repeated eigenvalue $\lambda$ but only one independent eigenvector $\mathbf{v}$. Then $e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}$ gives one solution and we need another, just as a repeated root needed $te^{rt}$. The answer looks similar, with one extra vector.

If $\lambda$ is a double eigenvalue with only one eigenvector $\mathbf{v}$, find a generalized eigenvector $\mathbf{w}$ with $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{v}$. Then $$\mathbf{x} = c_1e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v} + c_2e^{\lambda t}(t\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w}).$$

Try $\mathbf{x} = e^{\lambda t}(t\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w})$. Then $\mathbf{x}' = e^{\lambda t}(\lambda t\mathbf{v} + \lambda\mathbf{w} + \mathbf{v})$, while $A\mathbf{x} = e^{\lambda t}(t\lambda\mathbf{v} + A\mathbf{w})$. These match exactly when $A\mathbf{w} = \lambda\mathbf{w} + \mathbf{v}$, that is, $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{v}$. Such a $\mathbf{w}$ exists because $(A - \lambda I)^{2} = 0$ for a $2\times 2$ matrix with a double eigenvalue (Cayley–Hamilton), so the column space of $A - \lambda I$ is the eigenvector line. Any $\mathbf{w}$ works; adding a multiple of $\mathbf{v}$ only changes $c_1$.

blocks.title: A shortcut check
blocks.q: For the same $A$, write $A = 2I + N$ and compute $e^{2t}(I + tN)\mathbf{x}(0)$.
blocks.a: the same answer, through the matrix exponential

blocks.title: A degenerate node
steps: Every solution is $e^{-t}$ times a vector that grows at most like $t$, so it decays; trajectories come in tangent to the eigenvector line.

blocks.html: Writing $c_1e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v} + c_2te^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}$. That second term is not a solution: substituting it leaves an extra $e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}$ on the left. The correction $\mathbf{w}$ is exactly what absorbs it. Check by substituting into $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$.

blocks.cap: The first example: a single purple eigen-direction, and every other trajectory leaves the origin turning toward it. This is an unstable improper node.
